title: 2014 bird and bat post-construction monitoring report – Laurel Mountain Wind Energy Project
abstract:
Stantec Consulting Services Inc. (Stantec) conducted standardized post-construction bird and bat monitoring at the Laurel Mountain Wind Energy Project (Project) from 1 April to 15 November 2014. The work scope for year 2014 monitoring was developed in cooperation with AES Laurel Mountain, LLC (AESLM), the US Fish and Wildlife Service Elkins Field Office (USFWS), and the West Virginia Department of Natural Resources (WVDNR). Stantec searched 24 Project turbines at a 3 day interval and AESLM staff searched the remaining 37 turbines on a weekly basis.
All Project turbines were operated according to a sliding scale curtailment system developed for the Project by AESLM in coordination with the USFWS and WVDNR. This system was based on bat activity patterns documented from acoustic detector surveys in the rotor zone of Project turbines in fall 2011, spring/summer 2012, and spring – fall 2013, and feathered turbines fully during particular wind speed based on distribution of bat activity. Between 1 April and 15 November 2014, turbines were curtailed at night (30 minutes before sunset until 30 minutes after sunrise) based on wind speed . Under this system, turbine cut-in speeds were higher during and lower during such that turbines were fully feathered during conditions when most acoustic bat activity occurred at turbine height. In 2012 and 2013, the ceiling wind speed above which turbines operated without restriction, , was 8.5 meters per second (m/s) and the system was designed to avoid 99% of acoustic activity. This threshold was reduced to 6.9 m/s in 2014, and the 2014 system was also modified to include acoustic data collected in 2013. A total of 27 bat and 65 bird carcasses were documented during the 2014 monitoring period. No threatened or endangered bird or bat species or bats of the genus Myotis were found. Twentyone bat carcasses and 59 bird carcasses were found at the 24 study turbines monitored during standardized searches, and the rest were found at the 37 turbines searched by AESLM staff or found incidentally by Stantec. Fatality estimates for the 2014 monitoring period, based on the results at the 24 study turbines and taking into account search interval, carcass persistence, searcher efficiency, and an area correction factor, were 1.9 (95% CI 1.3 – 2.7) bats and 4.9 (95% CI 2.6 – 7.9) birds per turbine. The bat fatality rate for the 7.5 month 2014 monitoring period was 92% lower than the estimate for fully operational turbines based on the combined fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 6.5 month monitoring period (23.4 bats/turbine) and is estimated to be approximately 94% lower when normalized for equivalent monitoring periods. The 2014 estimates were within the 95% confidence intervals of estimates from 2013.

## **Executive Summary**

Stantec Consulting Services Inc. (Stantec) conducted standardized post-construction bird and bat monitoring at the Laurel Mountain Wind Energy Project (Project) from 1 April to 15 November 2014. The work scope for year 2014 monitoring was developed in cooperation with AES Laurel Mountain, LLC (AESLM), the US Fish and Wildlife Service Elkins Field Office (USFWS), and the West Virginia Department of Natural Resources (WVDNR). Stantec searched 24 Project turbines at a 3 day interval and AESLM staff searched the remaining 37 turbines on a weekly basis.

All Project turbines were operated according to a sliding scale curtailment system developed for the Project by AESLM in coordination with the USFWS and WVDNR. This system was based on bat activity patterns documented from acoustic detector surveys in the rotor zone of Project turbines in fall 2011, spring/summer 2012, and spring – fall 2013, and feathered turbines fully during particular (b) (4)

wind speed based on distribution of bat activity. Between 1 April and 15 November 2014, turbines were curtailed at night (30 minutes before sunset until 30 minutes after sunrise) based on (b) (4) wind speed (b) (4) . Under this system, turbine cut-in speeds were higher during (b) (4) and lower during (b) (4) such that turbines were fully feathered during conditions when most acoustic bat activity occurred at turbine height. In 2012 and 2013, the ceiling wind speed above which turbines operated without restriction, (b) (4) , was 8.5 meters per second (m/s) and the system was designed to avoid 99% of acoustic activity.  This threshold was reduced to 6.9 m/s in 2014, and the 2014 system was also modified to include acoustic data collected in 2013. A total of 27 bat and 65 bird carcasses were documented during the 2014 monitoring period. No threatened or endangered bird or bat species or bats of the genus _Myotis_ were found. Twentyone bat carcasses and 59 bird carcasses were found at the 24 study turbines monitored during standardized searches, and the rest were found at the 37 turbines searched by AESLM staff or found incidentally by Stantec. Fatality estimates for the 2014 monitoring period, based on the results at the 24 study turbines and taking into account search interval, carcass persistence, searcher efficiency, and an area correction factor, were 1.9 (95% CI 1.3 – 2.7) bats and 4.9 (95% CI 2.6 – 7.9) birds per turbine. The bat fatality rate for the 7.5 month 2014 monitoring period was 92% lower than the estimate for fully operational turbines based on the combined fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 6.5 month monitoring period (23.4 bats/turbine) and is estimated to be approximately 94% lower when normalized for equivalent monitoring periods. The 2014 estimates were within the 95% confidence intervals of estimates from 2013.

## **1.0 Introduction**

AES Laurel Mountain Wind, LLC (AESLM) began operation of the Laurel Mountain Wind Energy Project (Project) in Randolph and Barbour Counties, West Virginia in July 2011. Cut-in wind speeds of Project turbines have varied seasonally since the site became operational based on collaboration with the US Fish and Wildlife Service Elkins Field Office (USFWS) and WV Department of Natural Resources (WVDNR; Table 1-1). Stantec Consulting Services Inc. (Stantec) has conducted post-construction bird and bat fatality monitoring on a seasonal basis at the Project since mid-August 2011. Fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 monitoring involved comparison of 3 operational treatments: normally operating turbines with a factory cut-in speed of 3.5 meters per second (m/s; control turbines), turbines fully feathered below wind speeds of 3.5 m/s, and turbines fully feathered below wind speeds of 4.5 m/s. During fall 2012 and spring, summer, and fall 2013, all turbines were operated according to a sliding scale based on acoustic bat activity recorded on 6 turbine nacelles during fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012. Under this system, turbine cut-in speeds were higher (b) (4) and lower (b) (4)

such that turbines were fully feathered during conditions when 99% of acoustic bat activity occurred at turbine height. In 2012 and 2013, the ceiling wind speed above which turbines operated without restriction, (b) (4) , was 8.5 m/s.  This was reduced to 6.9 m/s in 2014, and the 2014 system was also modified to include additional acoustic data recorded at 6 turbines during fall 2012 and 9 turbines during year 2013 monitoring. The sliding-scale curtailment plan was implemented in early September through 15 November 2012, between 1 April and 15 November 2013, and again between 1 April and 15 November 2014 and was developed in coordination with the USFWS and WVDNR.

A work scope for year 2014 monitoring was presented to the USFWS and WVDNR on 27 February 2014. In coordination with AESLM, Stantec monitored 24 study turbines at a 3-day interval beginning 1 April 2014. AESLM developed a protocol for operations staff to conduct weekly surveys at the 37 turbines not surveyed by Stantec and initiated these surveys on 1 April 2014. This report summarizes results of standardized post-construction surveys conducted at the Project between 1 April and 15 November 2014.

## **1.1 STUDY AREA AND PROJECT DESCRIPTION**

The Project is a 97.6-megawatt (MW) facility located on private property leased to AESLM. The Project occupies 13 kilometers (km; 8 miles) of the ridgeline of Laurel Mountain in northeastern West Virginia (Figure 1-1). The Project is on the boundary between Randolph and Barbour Counties, near the town of Elkins, and consists of a linear ridgeline oriented northeast to southwest, with ridgetop elevations ranging from approximately 800 to 900 meters (m; 2,625 feet [’] to 2,953’). The western side of the ridgeline is more gradually sloped than the eastern side, which drops off steeply. The minimum elevation in the valleys surrounding Laurel Mountain is approximately 545 m (1,788’), resulting in an elevation differential of approximately 255 – 355 m (837’ – 1,165’) between valley and ridgetop.

Construction of the facility occurred between spring 2010 and mid-summer 2011, with the 61 1.6 MW GE XLE wind turbines becoming operational in July 2011. Each turbine has a hub height of 80 m (262’) and a rotor diameter of 82.5 m (271’), resulting in a maximum blade tip height of approximately 122 m (400’) and a rotor swept area (RSA) of approximately 5,343 m[2] (57,512 ft[2] ). Of the 61 turbines, 22 include a single synchronized flashing red light compliant with Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) standards. Turbines normally operate at wind speeds between approximately 3.5 m/s (7.8 miles per hour [mph]) and 20.0 m/s (56 mph), and rotate at speeds between 10 and 18 revolutions per minute (RPM).

In addition to the 61 turbines, the Project includes a single gravel access road running the length of the Project, an Operation and Maintenance (O&M) facility at the southern end of the Project, and 2 80-meter, guyed meteorological towers with flashing red lighting. The Project also includes an electrical substation and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), both of which are located near the midpoint of the Project where an existing utility-owned transmission line, utility-owned electrical switchyard, and county road cross the ridgeline.

## **2.0 Methods**

## **2.1 TURBINE OPERATIONAL PARAMETERS AND WEATHER DATA**

All Project turbines were controlled by a customized proprietary curtailment system developed by AESLM between 1 April and 15 November 2014 wherein turbines were fully feathered during (b) (4)

wind speed. Below cut-in conditions, turbine rotors were fully feathered so as to not rotate more than 1 RPM. Stantec confirmed turbine operation by determining the amount of time that turbines were rotating less than 1 RPM at wind speeds above 3.5 m/s, based on 10-minute resolution data provided AESLM at the conclusion of the survey period. In fall 2012 and 2013, the system was designed to allow turbine operation during (b) (4) wind speed where less than 1% of acoustic bat activity was documented (based on fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 acoustic survey results). In 2014, the sliding scale was updated to incorporate acoustic bat data from fall 2012 and April – November 2013. The system was also modified in 2014 to release turbines from curtailment at wind speeds greater than 6.9 m/s (b) (4) , (b) (4) regardless of wind speed (Table 2-1). This system was in place from 30 minutes before sunset through 30 minutes past sunrise from 1 April through 15 November 2014, with turbines operating normally outside of these periods.

## **2.3 FATALITY SURVEY METHODS**

Stantec conducted post-construction surveys at 3-day intervals at each of the 24 searched turbines. Unless prevented by inclement weather severe enough to compromise the safety of the surveyors or other factors preventing safe access to turbines, surveys occurred at a subset of searched turbines 7 days per week. The order in which turbines were searched and the direction in which surveyors walked transects varied among days. Surveyors maintained a steady, slow walking pace of approximately 35 – 45 m per minute (115 – 148’ per minute) along each marked transect, visually scanning the ground within 2 – 3 m (7 – 10’) of both sides of each transect. Although survey conditions changed between days based on weather, ground cover conditions and other factors, surveyors attempted to keep search times per turbine as consistent as possible among surveyors and survey days throughout the survey period. AESLM also mowed vegetation at searched turbines periodically during the monitoring period to maintain adequate visibility of the ground.

When a carcass was found during a survey, it was marked with a highly visible temporary marker, so that it was easily located for post-survey processing. Surveyors completed searching that particular turbine, marking any additional carcasses in a similar manner. At the conclusion of the turbine search, surveyors returned to inspect and process each carcass and recorded the distance and azimuth from the turbine to the carcass using a digital rangefinder and magnetic compass. Carcasses were identified in the field when possible and collected in a sealed plastic bag, labeled with a given carcass’ unique identification number and the information collected on-site at the time that carcass was found[1] . Surveyors recorded the date; time; turbine number; transect number; species, age, sex, and condition of carcass; distance and azimuth from turbine; general weather conditions such as cloud cover, precipitation and temperature; and any other notes regarding each carcass. Carcasses were stored in an off-site freezer owned by Stantec after the completion of daily surveys.

The general condition of each carcass was noted, including evidence of scavenging or presence of insects, to estimate freshness of the carcass. The amount of time since the fatality occurred was estimated based on the condition of the eyes and fur or feathers, the degree to which insect scavengers were present on the carcass, and the level of decomposition or desiccation. Carcasses were determined to be “fresh” if they had relatively intact plumage or pelage and little or no insect scavenging, such as removal of eyes. Visible signs of trauma such as broken wings or lacerations on a fresh carcass were also noted. Searchers took photos of each carcass. Carcasses determined to be _Myotis_ species or identified as potential _Myotis_ species were provided to biologists at the WVDNR for verification. Carcasses that were in too poor condition to be properly identified to species were classified as accurately as possible, or classified as “unknown.” Carcasses present at the beginning of the 2014 survey period that had obviously died prior to the survey periods were collected and identified, but were not included in estimates of total fatality.

1 Prior to AESLM’s receipt of a scientific collection permit on 9 June 2014 from the USFWS, Stantec did not handle or collect bird carcasses but left them in place. Fresh bird carcasses were treated as carcass removals during this period.

Carcasses found by Stantec searchers outside the daily search periods, outside the turbine search plots, or found by project operations staff and reported to Stantec, were considered incidental finds and were collected, identified, and stored according to the same protocols described above. As was done in 2013, incidental carcasses found within surveyed areas at the 24 searched turbines (during times when surveyors were on-site for other purposes or reported by AESLM personnel) were included in estimates of overall fatality as if they had been found during the next scheduled search, following the methods of Young et al. (2011) used at Mount Storm. Incidental carcasses found outside surveyed areas or at nonsearched turbines were not used in calculating overall estimated fatality rates.

In addition to Stantec’s post-construction monitoring, AESLM personnel conducted weekly bat carcass searches at the 37 turbines not searched by Stantec. AESLM staff reported any bat carcasses found during these surveys to Stantec, which then collected, and processed carcasses according to the methods described above. Any carcasses found by AESLM personnel at these 37 additional turbines were considered incidental carcasses and were not included in estimated fatality rates. Carcass searches conducted by AESLM were conducted to supplement standardized monitoring and detect rare mortality events.

## **2.3.1 Searcher Efficiency Trials**

Searcher efficiency trials were conducted throughout the survey period to quantify the ability of searchers to detect carcasses within the survey plots. Trial carcasses were placed at representative locations within search plots such that the searcher being tested was unaware that a trial was taking place. Searchers were unaware of the date and time of trials, and trial blindness was further ensured by varying the number of carcasses placed and the number of turbines with trial carcasses. Although trial carcasses were discreetly marked using a small piece of string tied around a leg to identify them as trial carcasses, searchers did not inspect the carcasses until the end of a turbine search. Searchers were therefore unaware that a trial had taken place until their turbine search was complete.

Searcher efficiency trials were conducted throughout the monitoring period, subject to carcass availability, with trials conducted in a variety of weather conditions. Trial coordinators predetermined the turbines at which carcasses were placed and selected trial locations that were representative of cover types in the search area. Carcasses were placed to ensure that the strings marking them as trials were only visible when the carcasses were picked up. Trial carcasses consisted of birds and bats found at Laurel Mountain, so composition of carcasses in terms of carcass size and ratio of birds or bats relied upon availability of carcasses found at the site. While most trial carcasses had been previously frozen, we selected carcasses in reasonably good condition for use in searcher efficiency trials. Brown mouse and juvenile quail carcasses were also used as trials when insufficient carcasses were available from the site. Trial carcasses were removed following each trial to prevent the loss of carcasses to scavengers, prevent potential attraction to the site by scavengers, and so that they would be available for use in subsequent trials.

Searcher efficiency (p) was expressed as the proportion of trial carcasses found by searchers: the number of trial carcasses successfully found by searchers divided by the total number of trial carcasses available during searcher efficiency trials. Trial carcasses removed by scavengers before the turbine was surveyed were considered invalid and were removed from the dataset. Trial carcasses that were found by the surveyor being tested were considered successful trials, and collected by that surveyor. Trial carcasses that were not found by the surveyor being tested were considered unsuccessful trials and were recovered by the trial coordinator, such that a surveyor had only one opportunity to find a trial carcass.

## **2.3.2 Carcass Removal Trials**

Carcass removal trials were conducted periodically throughout the survey period to quantify the length of time before carcasses were removed as well as to record qualitative information on the rate at which carcasses decomposed, dried, or were consumed by insects. During each trial, a carcass was placed in a known location at a given turbine, marked discreetly using a small piece of string, and monitored daily for the subsequent 14 days. Trials were placed at multiple turbines during the same trial period to provide a range of sampled locations and conditions. Carcasses were removed at the conclusion of the trial if still present. Observers recorded the date on which the carcass was entirely removed by scavengers or at which point the carcasses had decomposed or degraded beyond recognition.

Stantec conducted carcass removal trials throughout the monitoring period based on availability of carcasses, and made an effort to ensure that carcasses used in trials were of similar, relatively fresh condition, and had been handled minimally. Carcasses used during trials were birds and bats found during fatality surveys at Laurel Mountain, so carcass composition was dependent on fatality patterns at the site. While most carcasses used in trials had been previously frozen, we selected carcasses in as fresh condition as possible for carcass removal trials. Brown mouse and juvenile quail carcasses were also used as trials when insufficient carcasses were available from the site. Trial carcasses were placed at each searched turbine and in a variety of cover types and distances from turbines so that the combined trial dataset was representative of the variety of turbine locations and ground cover types present in the project area. Carcasses that were not present on the day following placement were considered to have been scavenged on day 1 of the trial and so on up to the 14th day of the trial, when carcasses that were still present were recovered.

Carcass persistence was calculated using a maximum likelihood estimator as employed by Erickson et al. (2003) and Good et al. (2011). The average number of days a carcass remained at a site before it was removed by scavengers (t) was expressed as:

## **2.4 DATA ANALYSIS AND ESTIMATED FATALITY RATES**

Estimates of total bird and bat fatality rates, adjusted for carcass removal rates, searcher efficiency, and area searched, followed the widely used method developed by Erikson et al. (2003), incorporating the Shoenfeld estimator for bias adjustment, as was done for fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 and 2013 surveys (Shoenfeld 2004). Mortality estimates were based only on carcasses found by Stantec during regular searches or found incidentally at regularly searched turbines. The same methods were used by Young et al. (2011) to calculate fatality estimates for surveys conducted at the NedPower Mount Storm Wind Energy Facility in northeastern West Virginia. Total estimated fatality was calculated separately for birds and bats within each operational treatment, and reported as a total number of mortalities per turbine per survey period. Fatality estimates were also reported per MW and per 1000 m[2] of RSA.

Searcher efficiency and scavenger removal trials were combined to derive a season-specific fatality adjustment ( _π_ ), using the following formula, where _I_ (the search interval) = 3, _p_ = the overall proportion of carcasses recovered in searcher efficiency trials, and _t_ = the mean number of days carcasses remained in the study area, as calculated above. This value represents the likelihood that a carcass would ultimately be found by searchers after multiple survey days, combining search interval, searcher efficiency, and carcass persistence rates. This value was calculated separately for birds and bats based on the results of searcher efficiency and scavenger removal trials for each group.

Fatality estimates were adjusted to account for area searched versus potential search area, and distribution of carcasses around turbines. A multiplier, _A_ , was calculated based on the percentage of area searched within 7 10-m bands surrounding each turbine, searcher efficiency, and numbers of carcasses found within each 10-m band. _A_ was calculated separately for birds and bats according to the following formula, as described in Young et al. (2011), where _ck_ equals the number of carcasses within the k[th] distance band, _p_ equals searcher efficiency, and _sk_ equals the proportion of area searched within the k[th] distance band across searched turbines.

Total fatality ( _m_ ), representing the number of mortalities estimated per turbine for the corresponding survey period, was then estimated separately for birds and bats using the following equation, where _c_ = the mean number of fatalities documented per turbine, _A_ = the area correction, and _π_ adjusts for searcher efficiency and scavenger removal rates. Incidental carcasses found at the 24 searched turbines outside normal survey times were included in fatality estimates although other incidental carcasses were excluded.

Bootstrapping methods were used to determine 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) surrounding each estimate, which were established using quantiles of the bootstrapped samples (Erickson et al. 2003, Young et al. 2011). CI for searcher efficiency were calculated by choosing 5,000 random samples (with replacement) from the trial data set and calculating a searcher efficiency rate for each sample. CI for carcass persistence rates were calculated by choosing 5,000 random samples (with replacement) from the trial data set and calculating a carcass persistence rate for each sample. An additional 5,000 samples of observed fatality were derived by choosing a random set of turbines 5,000 times and summing the total number of carcasses found at each turbine in the sample. The fatality adjustment ( _π_ ) and total fatality ( _m_ ) were calculated for each bootstrapped sample.

## **3.0 Results**

## **3.1 TURBINE OPERATIONAL PARAMETERS**

Turbines at the Project operated according to the customized cut-in wind speed curtailment system described in Section 2.1 on a nightly basis between 1 April and 15 November 2014. The amount of time turbines were actually curtailed (rotor speed < 1 RPM) while wind speeds were greater than 3.5 m/s depended on actual wind (b) (4) conditions measured at the site. The 24 turbines monitored between 1 April and 15 November 2014 were curtailed for an average of 934 (±87 SD) hours per turbine cumulatively during the survey period. By month, turbines were curtailed for the greatest number of hours during July, with an average of 174 hours (±9 SD) of curtailment per turbine (Figure 3-1).

## **3.2.2 Species Composition**

Including all carcasses found at the 24 study turbines and 37 non-study turbines in 2014, 27 bat and 65 bird carcasses were collected at the Project. Four bat species were documented including eastern red bat, silver-haired bat, hoary bat, and big brown bat (Table 3-2). Long-distance migratory species accounted for 96% of bat carcasses found in 2014. No Myotis species or unknown bats were found. Of the 27 total bat carcasses, 11 (41%) were male, 4 (15%) were female, and 12 (44%) were of an unknown sex. Twenty-two bird species were documented including yellow-rumped warbler, red-tailed hawk, golden-crowned kinglet, and red-eyed vireo (Table 3-3). No threatened or endangered bird or bat species were found during 2014 surveys.

## **3.2.3 Searcher Efficiency Trials**

Stantec placed 40 bat carcasses and 32 bird carcasses during searcher efficiency trials. Due to a small number of carcasses available for searcher efficiency trials, Stantec obtained additional carcasses from a lab supply company. These include 51 brown mouse carcasses, which were grouped with bat carcasses for analysis purposes, and 39 juvenile quail carcasses, for a total of 162 attempted searcher efficiency trials during the 2014 monitoring period. Of these, 8 bat/mouse carcasses and 3 bird carcasses were removed by scavengers during the trial period and were removed from the dataset resulting in 83 valid bat/mouse and 68 valid bird searcher efficiency trials. Trials were placed on 14 separate occasions between 15 April and 11 November. Searchers recovered 39 bat/mouse trial carcasses (47%) and 40 bird trial carcasses (59%) during the 2014 monitoring period.

Trial carcasses were placed at 22 different turbines and 72 (44%) consisted of birds and bats found previously at the site. As such, trial carcasses were considered representative of the types and sizes of carcasses typically found at the Project. Trial carcasses were placed in a variety of ground cover conditions, and at variable distances and azimuths from turbines to accurately represent the range of ground cover types and conditions present at searched turbines.

## **3.2.4 Carcass Removal Trials**

Stantec conducted 106 carcass removal trials during the 2014 monitoring period using bat (n = 16) and bird (n = 58) carcasses found previously on-site and in relatively good condition, and mouse (n = 11) and juvenile quail (n = 21) carcasses obtained from a lab supply company. Mouse carcasses were grouped with bat carcasses for analysis purposes, for a total of 27 bat/mouse carcasses and 79 bird carcasses. Carcass removal trials began on 7 separate days between 6 April and 1 October 2014, each lasting 14 days. Of the 106 carcasses placed, 26 (25%) were removed on the first day of the trial period, 73 (69%) were removed by the 7[th] day, and 85 (80%) were removed before the 14[th] day of the trial period (Figure 3-8). Carcasses were removed by scavengers between the 1[st] and 13[th] day of trials. Six bat/mouse carcasses and 15 bird carcasses remained throughout the entire 14 day trial period.

## **4.0 Discussion**

## **4.1 TURBINE OPERATION**

The customized cut-in wind speed curtailment system appeared to perform as designed throughout the 2014 monitoring period. Comparison of turbine RPM during particular (b) (4) wind speed during the day and at night for the 24 study turbines indicated that turbines were feathered during the conditions specified in the sliding scale developed for the site in cooperation with the USFWS and WVDNR. No faults of the system were reported by AESLM during the monitoring period.

Figure 4-1 shows a comparison of the average number of hours turbines were curtailed in 2014 to the average number of hours turbines were curtailed in 2013. Turbines were curtailed for an average of 20% fewer hours in 2014. In 2013, turbines were curtailed for the greatest number of hours in August, with an average of 231 hours (±14 SD) of curtailment per turbine. In August 2014, turbines were curtailed for an average of 160 hours (±18 SD), which is 31% fewer hours than in August 2013.

conditions and the same seasonal time period. Monitoring during fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 enabled comparison of 3 operational scenarios, each with 8 turbines. During the fall 2012 and year 2013 and 2014 monitoring periods, all searched turbines were operated under the same operational scheme designed to avoid potential impacts to listed bat species. Table 4-1 summarizes fatality estimates for birds and bats derived from each distinct monitoring period, highlighting estimates that are most relevant for comparing among survey years.

Bat fatality estimates have differed substantially among monitoring periods at the Project, due primarily to the variable curtailment parameters used in fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 versus fall 2012 and year 2013 and 2014. The bat fatality estimate most representative of fully operational turbines was 23.4 bats/turbine derived from the control turbines in the combined fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 monitoring period (6.5 months of monitoring). The estimate of 1.9 bats/turbine for the 2014 monitoring period was 92% less than the 2011/2012 control estimate, and included the full 7.5 months between 1 April and 15 November. For comparison purposes only, we simulated a mortality rate for a full 7.5 month period at control turbines in 2011 by multiplying the 2011 estimate of 23.4 bats/turbine by a scaling factor of 1.3 to account for carcasses found during the first two weeks of August and the first two weeks of November 2011, assuming constant mortality rates between 1 – 31 August and 15 October 2011 and 15 November 2011. This process yielded a simulated estimate of 30.8 bats/turbine, suggesting that the 2014 curtailment system may have reduced bat mortality by as much as 94% relative to fully operational turbines[2] .

Spatial distribution of carcasses in 2014 was similar to that documented in previous survey periods. Carcass persistence was slightly greater for bats and slightly less for birds in 2014 relative to the fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 survey period, when carcasses persistence was estimated to be 6.6 days (95% CI 5.2 – 8.4) for bats and 7.1 days (95% CI 5.2 – 9.7) for birds. Carcass persistence was slightly greater in 2014 compared to the 2013 survey period, when carcass persistence was estimated to be 5.9 days (95% CI 4.5 – 8.0) for bats and 4.4 days (95% CI 3.2 – 6.2) for birds.

Searcher efficiency estimates during the 2014 monitoring period were similar to those from the fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 monitoring period and the 2013 monitoring period. Searcher efficiency was slightly higher for bats than birds during previous monitoring periods and slightly higher for birds than bats during the 2014 monitoring period. Higher searcher efficiency for birds in 2014 could be the result of a greater number of medium-sized birds placed during trials. Periodic mowing of vegetation at the study turbines by AESLM maintained good visibility of the ground.

## **4.4 CURTAILMENT EVALUATION**

Based on the low bat fatality estimates derived in fall 2012 and years 2013 and 2014, the customized sliding scale curtailment system appears highly effective at reducing risk of bat fatality at Laurel Mountain. The bat fatality estimate was 92% less than estimated from fully operational turbines at the site based on a shorter monitoring period, and is estimated to be approximately 94% lower when normalized for equivalent monitoring periods. The number of bat carcasses found per turbine was generally consistent among monitored turbines, indicating little inter-turbine variability in effectiveness of the system. As no turbines at Laurel Mountain were fully operational during 2014, the “control” estimates derived from the combined fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012 period provide the best data for comparison. The curtailment system was reliable and AES noted no failures of the automated system at any turbine throughout the 1 April – 15 November 2014 study period.

The USFWS established a goal of reducing overall bat fatality rates by 95% relative to the estimate for control turbines at this site as a way to demonstrate avoidance of risk of protected species fatalities. While the reduction in mortality due to the curtailment system cannot be tested directly without comparison to un-curtailed control turbines monitored during the same interval, the 2014 mortality estimate was 92% lower than that estimated for control turbines during a shorter (6.5 month) monitoring period at this site in fall 2011 and spring/summer 2012. AESLM feels that the modified curtailment system is effective at its intended purpose of avoiding potential mortality of _Myotis_ species.
